text:
Lucian Santangelo (VP of People): Thank you for returning my call. I regret to say that we must suspend the project.
Rep: I am sorry to hear it. May I ask what has happened?
Lucian Santangelo (VP of People): Certainly. Our parent company announced a reorganisation on Monday. Three of the four regional offices are to be consolidated, and my own role is, shall we say, under discussion. In that climate, no one is prepared to approve a new payroll system.
Signe Zeller (Payroll Manager): I can confirm that. I was told yesterday that every open initiative is on hold until the structure is settled. Our current system will simply continue.
Rep: Have you spoken with any other provider?
Lucian Santangelo (VP of People): No. None. We have not engaged anyone. I should like to be clear that your demonstration and your proposal were both excellent, and the figures were within what we had expected.
Signe Zeller (Payroll Manager): Nothing about the product was at issue.
Rep: Would it be acceptable to contact you after the reorganisation concludes?
Lucian Santangelo (VP of People): I should welcome that, though I cannot say whether I shall still be here. Signe will know.

Hollis Ashgrove (Head of HR): Thank you for the proposal, and for your patience while we reviewed it. I will be candid with you about where we have arrived.
Rep: Please. I would value that.
Hollis Ashgrove (Head of HR): The annual cost does not fit our budget. Your proposal comes to approximately twenty-six thousand dollars for the year, which, across our 132 employees, is about two hundred dollars per head. The budget we were allocated for this entire category is nearer eighteen thousand.
Rep: And is there an alternative that falls within that?
Hollis Ashgrove (Head of HR): There is. Tallyhold has quoted us just under seventeen thousand, around one hundred and thirty per employee. It is not as polished, I will concede that. But it is within the number our managing director gave us.
Noor Ivarsson (Compliance Lead): From my side, I examined the compliance features in your product and I was satisfied. I want that on the record. The reporting for our two states was sound.
Hollis Ashgrove (Head of HR): Correct. The difficulty is not the product. It is the sum on the invoice.
Rep: Would a smaller package, or a phased start, help?
Hollis Ashgrove (Head of HR): I appreciate the offer. I put the same question to our managing director, and the answer was that the ceiling is the ceiling. I do not believe a modest reduction would close a gap of that size.
Noor Ivarsson (Compliance Lead): We would recommend your company to others, though, at a different stage.
Rep: Thank you both. I appreciate the directness.
Hollis Ashgrove (Head of HR): The pleasure was ours. We shall be in touch should our circumstances change.

Subject: Our decision

Dear team,

Thank you for your proposal. Regrettably, at roughly $26,000 a year it exceeds the budget we have for this, and we have accepted a quote near $17,000 from another provider. The product itself impressed us. We wish you well.

Sincerely,
Hollis Ashgrove

Omar Castellane (People Operations Lead): Hey. Sorry, I just got off another call, I'm a bit fried.
Rep: No worries. Thanks for jumping on.
Omar Castellane (People Operations Lead): So. We're going a different direction. I wanted to say it out loud instead of sending a form email.
Rep: I appreciate that. Is there anything you can share about the decision?
Omar Castellane (People Operations Lead): Not really. It's just where we landed. We're making a change. That's about all I've got in me today, honestly.
Omar Abernethy (General Manager): Yeah, I'll back him on that. No drama. You were good to deal with.
Rep: Thanks. And if anything comes up later?
Omar Castellane (People Operations Lead): Sure. Keep in touch. Really.
Omar Abernethy (General Manager): Send a note now and then. We don't bite.
Rep: I will. Take care of yourselves.
Omar Castellane (People Operations Lead): You too. I need coffee.
Omar Abernethy (General Manager): Get some sleep, Omar.
Omar Castellane (People Operations Lead): Ha. Thanks, boss.

Subject: Thanks for everything

Hi,

I wanted to follow up our call with a note. Thank you for all the time you and your team spent with us. We've decided to go a different direction and won't be moving forward. I know that's not the answer you were hoping for, and I'm sorry to leave you without more detail. The folks you worked with on our side enjoyed the conversations, and I hope we can stay in touch. Wishing you a good rest of the year.

Best,
Omar

Ingrid Parekh (Head of HR): We're not going ahead. Let me say why.
Rep: Please.
Ingrid Parekh (Head of HR): It's the yearly cost. You came in around thirty-four thousand. That's about two hundred a head for 167 people. We have twenty-five set aside. Tallyhold came in at about twenty-two. That's the whole story.
Emeka Thorsen (Head of People): I'd like a bigger number to work with, I really would. I like your product. But the COO signs off and she won't go past twenty-five.
Rep: Was there anything on the product side that held you back?
Ingrid Parekh (Head of HR): No. It's the number.
Emeka Thorsen (Head of People): Also, small thing, the demo was eleven days after the first call. That was a long wait. But it didn't change the answer. Even if it had been next day, we'd still be here.
Ingrid Parekh (Head of HR): Right. It's the number.
Rep: Could we revisit scope?
Ingrid Parekh (Head of HR): We looked. Still too far.
Emeka Thorsen (Head of People): Thanks for being decent about it.

Thaddeus Hartigan (COO): Oh, hey, hi. I was hoping to catch you before you sent the contract. So, I hate this part, but I'll just say it. It's the money. Your yearly number is around twenty-seven thousand, and for a hundred and eighteen people that's, what, nineteen bucks a head a month, and I've got a competing quote from Tallyhold for about seventeen thousand. Which is like twelve a head. Ten thousand dollars! I can't un-see it.
Rep: I understand.
Idris Thorsen (Operations Director): And I told Thaddeus, we should pay for the better thing, I really did, and he said, Idris, I've got the budget my CFO gave me and it's twenty, and that's that. So there we are.
Thaddeus Hartigan (COO): Twenty, maybe twenty-two. Don't hate me.
Rep: Not at all.
Rep: Can I follow up in a month, in case anything shifts?
Thaddeus Hartigan (COO): Sure, sure. Call me. I'll pick up. I just can't do anything this quarter.
Idris Thorsen (Operations Director): Yeah, call us.
Rep: Great, I'll put a note on the calendar.

Lucian Thorsen (Chief People Officer): I wish to be candid. It may sound unreasonable, but even the single day between our first call and your demonstration proved too long for us. The idea had a champion on Tuesday, and by Wednesday afternoon that champion was fully occupied elsewhere. I had already asked my team to begin on an alternative, and by the time you presented we had two weeks of work behind us.
Rep: One day. I admit I had not thought that long.
Lucian Thorsen (Chief People Officer): Nor had I, until I saw how quickly the mood in the room changed.
Rafferty Fairweather (Benefits Manager): There is a further matter, though a minor one. Our finance sponsor left the company last week, and the project has lost its principal voice. I do not believe that was decisive. The earlier shift had already occurred.
Lucian Thorsen (Chief People Officer): I agree. It was the pace of events, and the alternative was already in progress.
Rep: I understand. Thank you for telling me.
Lucian Thorsen (Chief People Officer): Thank you for the courtesy.

Emeka Brannigan (VP of People): Short and practical. We're stopping. For now.
Rep: Okay. What changed?
Emeka Brannigan (VP of People): We lost a big contract. Two weeks ago. Eleven percent of our revenue, gone with a phone call. Leadership shifted every dollar to keeping the crews employed. Anything not touching a rig or a truck is on ice.
Kwame Vasquez (Operations Director): That includes payroll software. I pushed. They said, show me the ROI after we replace the contract. Fair, I guess.
Rep: Have you looked at anyone else?
Emeka Brannigan (VP of People): No. Nobody. We're sticking with what we have, the old system and a lot of manual cleanup. It's ugly. But it's not on fire.
Kwame Vasquez (Operations Director): I'd like to be clear that it isn't about you. Your demo was the best we saw. The reporting was clean, the plan was solid, and your quote was reasonable.
Emeka Brannigan (VP of People): Agreed. I'd have signed in September.
Rep: When might this thaw?
Emeka Brannigan (VP of People): My guess is spring at the earliest. Maybe summer. It depends on the pipeline. The CEO said he'd revisit in April.
Kwame Vasquez (Operations Director): Keep us warm. Don't pester. A check-in in March would be good.
Rep: Will do. Thanks for telling me straight.

Fenella Brannigan (HR Director): Thank you for joining on short notice. I owe you an update, and I am afraid it is not the one either of us hoped for.
Rep: I appreciate you telling me directly. What is the situation?
Fenella Brannigan (HR Director): The company has decided to reconsider its priorities for the coming year. Our leadership has asked every department to identify its top two initiatives, and a payroll migration did not make the list. Instead, the focus is on a facilities consolidation, which will absorb both budget and attention across five states.
Marisol Hollander (IT Manager): From my side, my team has been asked to support the consolidation through the spring. We simply do not have the capacity to take on an integration project in parallel. I raised it twice and the answer was the same.
Rep: Has your team looked at any alternative providers?
Fenella Brannigan (HR Director): We have not. We have not engaged anyone. The existing arrangement will continue. I should say plainly that your presentation and your proposal were both considered excellent, and that nothing in them gave us pause.
Marisol Hollander (IT Manager): That is correct. I had no concerns with the technical documentation.
Rep: Might I contact you again in the new year?
Fenella Brannigan (HR Director): Yes, please. I would suggest after the consolidation is complete. I expect the picture to be clearer by then.

Subject: Postponing our payroll project

Dear team,

Thank you for your time and for the clear proposal. Our leadership has redirected its priorities toward a facilities consolidation, and the payroll project has been postponed. We have not selected another provider, and the decision does not reflect on your product or the proposal. I would be glad to reconnect once the consolidation is complete.

Sincerely,
Fenella Brannigan

Kwame Hartigan (COO): So I'll be honest, I've been awake since five, so excuse me if I'm blunt. We're not going with you, and it's the reporting.
Rep: Tell me more about what you needed.
Kwame Hartigan (COO): Every quarter I have to put a package together for the board. Headcount by plant, overtime as a percent of labor cost, turnover by department, and they like to slice it differently every time. Last quarter somebody wanted it by shift and tenure band. In the demo, I asked how I'd build that, and the answer was, here are the twelve standard reports, and you can export to a spreadsheet.
Lucian Delacroix (Head of Finance): Which I can do. I do it now. It's the thing I'm trying to stop doing. I spend two days every quarter in a spreadsheet pulling it together.
Rep: And Corvane handles it differently?
Kwame Hartigan (COO): They've got a report builder. Drag and drop. It's not perfect, but I can make the board's weird slices myself without calling anybody.
Lucian Delacroix (Head of Finance): For the record, the price was fine. The tax filing piece was fine. It's just reporting.
Kwame Hartigan (COO): It's a shame, honestly. I liked your people.
Rep: If we shipped a builder, would you want to hear?
Kwame Hartigan (COO): Sure. Send me a note. I'll be too tired to be mad.

Subject: Our decision

Hi,

Thanks for the time. We've decided to go with another provider. The deciding factor was reporting: we need to build flexible, custom views for our quarterly board package without exporting to spreadsheets, and that wasn't there. Everything else looked good. If that changes, let us know.

Kwame

Fenella Petrakis (HR Generalist): Quick update, and it's not great news. The project is on hold.
Rep: I'm sorry. What happened?
Fenella Petrakis (HR Generalist): Our owner is in the middle of selling a majority stake. It was announced Friday. Until the deal closes, the buyers have asked us to avoid any major system changes. Nothing new, nothing replaced.
Fenella Fairweather (HR Director): That's the long and short of it. I've been told to hold anything that isn't already running. We're 179 people in five states, and if the sale goes through, the new owners might want us on their system anyway.
Rep: Have you spoken with anyone else?
Fenella Petrakis (HR Generalist): No one. We haven't selected anything. We're staying where we are until we know.
Rep: Was anything about our proposal an issue?
Fenella Fairweather (HR Director): Not at all. It was a good proposal. The price was fine.
Fenella Petrakis (HR Generalist): Small thing, and I mean small: it took four days to get from our first call to the demo, which I'd have liked faster, but that isn't what happened here. It's the sale.
Fenella Fairweather (HR Director): Agreed. If we'd done it in one day, we'd still be paused.
Rep: Could I follow up in a few months?
Fenella Petrakis (HR Generalist): Yes. Give it until spring. We should know by then.

Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): Straight to it. We're pausing.
Rep: Understood. What happened?
Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): Our CEO resigned on Monday. Board brought in an interim. First thing she did was freeze new projects. Everything.
Kofi Brannigan (Compliance Lead): Including ours. I was supposed to start the data cleanup this week. Told to stop.
Rep: Did you pick another provider?
Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): No. Nobody. We're not even talking to anyone.
Kofi Brannigan (Compliance Lead): We liked the demo. I want you to know that. Nothing was wrong with it.
Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): Same. Good product. Fair terms. Bad timing, that's all.
Rep: When do you expect clarity?
Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): Maybe three months. Maybe six. A permanent CEO takes time.
Rep: May I reach out in the spring?
Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): Do. Ask for me or Kofi.
Kofi Brannigan (Compliance Lead): Honestly, I'll miss the weekly calls. The setup walkthrough you gave us was useful.
Rep: That's kind. I'll hold everything we discussed on file so we can pick it up where we left off.
Odalys Yarrow (Chief People Officer): Appreciated. Thank you for understanding.

Annelise Whitlock (COO): Thank you for your patience while we deliberated. I would like to be direct about our conclusion.
Rep: Please do.
Annelise Whitlock (COO): The annual cost does not fit our budget. Your proposal is approximately thirty-eight thousand dollars for the year. For our 168 employees, that is around two hundred and twenty-five dollars each. Tallyhold has proposed roughly twenty-five thousand, or about one hundred and fifty per employee. The difference is thirteen thousand, and my board will not accept it.
Bastian Thorsen (Head of People): I would like to add that I argued for your platform. The experience is better. But I cannot defend a fifty percent premium to the board.
Rep: Is there flexibility in what you would need from us?
Annelise Whitlock (COO): We considered it. I will mention, as a secondary matter, that we had hoped to manage applicant tracking in the same system, and your platform does not provide it. Tallyhold offers a basic module. That was a consideration, though a minor one. It was not the deciding factor.
Bastian Thorsen (Head of People): Correct. The cost remains the principal obstacle.
Rep: I understand. Thank you for your candour.
Annelise Whitlock (COO): Thank you for your professionalism. We may reconsider if our budget changes next year.

Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): Thanks for hopping on. I'll keep this short. We're putting the project down.
Rep: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me what happened?
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): Yeah. Our biggest customer, a developer, delayed a phase of their build. Six months. That's a third of our work for the year. Overnight.
Soren Delacroix (Operations Director): I took the call. The owner and I sat down the same afternoon. We went line by line through spending. Anything that wasn't keeping a crew on a job got cut or deferred.
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): Which is how payroll software ended up in the deferred pile. It's a shame. I wanted this.
Rep: Have you looked at any other providers in the meantime?
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): No. None. We haven't talked to anyone else. We're staying on what we've got.
Soren Delacroix (Operations Director): It's painful. We're 131 people across five states and the current setup has me re-keying hours from timesheets every other Friday. I'd love to stop. But I can't ask for a budget line this quarter.
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): I told Soren, your demo was clean. Your price was fair. The implementation plan made sense. I'd have signed it.
Soren Delacroix (Operations Director): We both would have.
Rep: When might things loosen up?
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): The developer says the phase restarts in the summer. If they hold to it, we'll be hiring again by then, and then we'll need the system more than ever.
Soren Delacroix (Operations Director): I'd say call us in June.
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): Yeah. June. And thanks for not being pushy. It's appreciated. Last time a vendor called me, I was on a roof.
Soren Delacroix (Operations Director): He really was on a roof.
Rep: Of course. I'll keep your materials ready.
Soren Delacroix (Operations Director): Appreciate it.
Kwame Jessamy (Operations Manager): Talk to you in June.

Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): Hi. Sorry, it's been a day. Three fire drills and a flooded supply closet.
Rep: That sounds like a lot. Should we reschedule?
Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): No, no. Better to get it over with. So. We've decided to go a different direction.
Rep: Okay. Thank you for saying so. Would you mind sharing anything about how you came to that?
Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): I don't think I can add much. It's where we ended up. We're making a change.
Ingrid Ashgrove (HR Director): Yes, I'd say the same. It's just the direction we're going.
Rep: Understood. I hope the demo and the materials were at least useful.
Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): Very. Everyone was great. I'm tired, not annoyed. Please don't read anything into it.
Ingrid Ashgrove (HR Director): Honestly the whole team was a pleasure to deal with.
Rep: That's kind. Could I check in once in a while?
Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): Sure. Once in a while. Nothing aggressive.
Ingrid Ashgrove (HR Director): A holiday card would be fine.
Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): Ha. Yes. With a gift basket, if you're feeling generous.
Rep: I'll see what the budget allows.
Oriel Yarrow (Office Manager): Okay. I should go find a mop.
Ingrid Ashgrove (HR Director): Thanks again, both.
Rep: Take care. Good luck with the closet.

Subject: Thank you

Hi,

Thanks for taking the time to walk us through everything, and for being so patient with our questions. We've decided to go a different direction, so we won't be moving forward. It was a pleasure working with you, and everyone here appreciated the care you took. I hope we cross paths again.

All the best,
Oriel

Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): We're going with Tallyhold.
Rep: Thanks for telling me. Can I ask what drove it?
Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): Our broker. She recommended them. She's handled our renewals for years. I'm not going to go against her.
Rep: Did she say why?
Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): She put the bundle in front of us. Payroll, benefits, time tracking, one price. She said it fits our size. A hundred and eighteen people, two states. I trust her.
Ingrid Thorsen (IT Manager): I'll chip in. I looked at both from the technical side. You were fine. It wasn't a technical call. It was a relationship call.
Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): Right. Our broker negotiates with the carriers every year. If something breaks in open enrollment, she's the one who fixes it. If we're on her pick, she's accountable. If we're not, I'm on my own.
Rep: That makes sense. Is there anything in the product that you'd flag?
Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): Not really. One thing, small. The carrier files. Your system doesn't send them automatically. Hers does, I think. That would be nice. But that's not why.
Ingrid Thorsen (IT Manager): It's a nice-to-have. We'd have lived without it.
Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): The broker is the reason. Our broker. That's it.
Rep: Understood. Thank you for being straight.
Sunniva Delacroix (Operations Manager): Of course. You were good to work with.

Subject: Thank you, and a note for your broker

Hi Sunniva,

Thank you for letting me know, and for the candor on our call. I understand that your broker's recommendation carried the decision, and that the bundle she put together fit how you already work with her. That kind of trust is hard to build, and I respect it. I also took note of your comment about automatic carrier files. It's useful feedback for our product team. If your situation changes at your next renewal, or if you'd ever like a second opinion on payroll, I'd be glad to talk. Wishing you and Ingrid a smooth transition.

Best,
Your Lanternmere HR rep

Kofi Jessamy (People Operations Lead): Okay, so, where do I even start. I guess with the thing I don't want you to take the wrong way. We're not buying anything. Not you, not anybody.
Rep: Oh, I see. What happened?
Kofi Jessamy (People Operations Lead): So our founder, who was the one pushing this, he stepped back last month. Health thing. He's okay, he's fine, but he's out, and the board doesn't want to commit to anything big until they've figured out who's running things day to day. And, well, I'd been hoping it would just keep going on its own steam, but nobody's picking it up.
Idris Valdivia (Head of People): Yeah, and I'd love to tell you we're different, but I'm in the same boat. They told me, no new vendors until the new year, at least. Maybe longer. I've got a hundred and three people across five states on a system that makes me want to cry, but my hands are tied.
Rep: Did anything about our offer give you pause?
Kofi Jessamy (People Operations Lead): No, no, nothing. You were great. Hm, okay, one small thing I'll say, the wait between the first call and the demo was fifteen days, which, yeah, was a bit long, but we were busy too, and I don't think it changed anything. It's not that.
Idris Valdivia (Head of People): It's the founder situation. That's all.
Rep: Could I check back in January?
Kofi Jessamy (People Operations Lead): Oh please, yes. January. February maybe. Ha, I'm hedging, aren't I.

Rep: Amara, Priya, thanks for making time. Where would you like to start?
Amara Hollander (Operations Manager): Taxes. We have people in six states and honestly that's the whole conversation. Let me give you a real one. We have two adjusters who live in Virginia and work out of our Maryland office. Another lives in Maryland and drives into DC. How does your system handle withholding for those, given the reciprocity?
Rep: So we support the reciprocity setups in the common state pairs, and you'd file the exemption certificates...
Amara: Which pairs, specifically? Virginia and DC, DC and Maryland?
Rep: I'd want to confirm the exact list with our tax team. I think those are covered, but we'd have to check.
Priya Underhill (CFO): Second one. An underwriter moved from Ohio to Kentucky in July. She worked remotely the whole time. Ohio municipal tax was withheld January through June. What does the system do in August when her address changes?
Rep: It updates the state, and I believe the local, but I'd have to check on how the Ohio municipal piece stops.
Priya: That piece costs us money if it's wrong. We've been burned. And who registers us with each state, you or us? And who files the quarterly returns?
Rep: We file in most states once you're registered. The registration step I'd need to get back to you on.
Amara: Look, I'll say it once, the price is fine. It's a little higher than Corvane's quote, and I can live with that. What I can't live with is hearing 'we'd have to check' on withholding for a quarter of my staff.
Priya: We're a licensed insurance business. Audits aren't theoretical for us.
Rep: Understood. I can get you written answers by Friday.
Amara: Send them. But I'll be straight, we're leaning the other way.

Rep: Morning, Imani, Nadia. Let's get into it.
Imani Fairweather (Office Manager): Quick one first. You took a week to get us the demo. I'm not mad, I'm just noting it. Anyway, we're in nine states, and that's what I care about. Show me taxes.
Rep: Sure. Our engine calculates state withholding, unemployment, and the local pieces where they apply.
Imani: Okay, scenario. A developer moved from Colorado to Oregon in June. Same job, fully remote. What does payroll do on the first check after the address change?
Rep: It switches the state withholding. For Oregon's transit tax, I'd need to confirm whether it picks that up automatically. We'd have to check.
Nadia Valdivia (Compliance Lead): And Colorado's family leave premiums, do they stop? Do we owe anything for the first half?
Rep: The premiums for the months worked there stay on the record. The rest I'd take back to the tax team.
Nadia: Second scenario. We hire our first person in Tennessee next quarter. Do you register us with the state for unemployment, or do we do it ourselves and then give you the account number?
Rep: Typically you'd register and we'd load the number. I'm not certain whether we offer registration assistance.
Imani: See, that's the answer I keep getting. Price is fine, by the way. Honestly it's close to what Corvane quoted. I wouldn't change my mind on that.
Nadia: With nine states, one miss means a notice from some state agency, and then I'm the one answering it.
Rep: I'll send you a written breakdown by state.
Imani: Please do. We're probably going elsewhere, though.

Rep: Idris, Wren, good afternoon. Thank you both for joining. I wanted to use the time to see where you are after the demo.
Idris Vasquez (Head of HR): Thank you for having us again. And for the time your team has put in. It has been a pleasure working with everyone.
Rep: Likewise. Is there anything from the walkthrough I can clarify, or anything we can send over to help your review?
Idris: That is kind of you. I think we have what we need. I should be transparent that we have decided to go in a different direction.
Rep: I appreciate you telling me directly. Would it be helpful to hear what we might do differently?
Idris: Not at all, the process was very professional. We simply feel we are making a change, and that is where we have landed.
Wren Parekh (Finance Director): If I may add, we are grateful for the proposal and for everything you shared. Please pass our thanks to the implementation team as well.
Rep: I will. Is it all right if I check back in a few months?
Idris: Certainly. We would be glad to hear from you. We wish you the very best.
Rep: Same to you both. I hope the new year goes well for the company.
Idris: Thank you. Take care.
Wren: Take care.

Rep: Delphine, Greta, thanks for joining. I know last week was busy.
Delphine Jessamy (COO): It was, and it's why I wanted this call. I'd rather tell you in person than let it go quiet. We're pausing. Not you, not anyone. The whole thing is paused.
Rep: Can you tell me what happened?
Delphine: Sure. On the second of the month the board froze discretionary spend through at least the end of Q2. The Harlan Street project came in about 1.4 million over, and every initiative that wasn't tied to revenue got shelved. This is on the list. Ours was line nine of eleven.
Greta Nakamura (VP Finance): I want to add, I was the one who pushed to get this started. Mina, who sponsored it, left in the middle of last month. So there's nobody above me who has the appetite to reopen it right now.
Rep: That makes sense. Are you evaluating anyone else in the meantime?
Delphine: No. We're staying on our current payroll provider and the spreadsheets. We haven't signed with anyone and we haven't called anyone else. I'd tell you if we had.
Greta: The demo was good, for what it's worth. Our compliance questions were answered. It's simply a question of whether we spend money at all this year.
Rep: Would it help if I checked back in January?
Delphine: Yes. Try the second week. By then we'll know whether the freeze lifts.

Rep: Linnea, Priya, good morning. Thank you for the time.
Linnea Underhill (Operations Manager): Good morning. I will be direct about our concern, if I may. We have employees in four states, and one of them is Pennsylvania. Our largest site is in Allegheny County, and we have people who live in other municipalities. Local earned income tax is, frankly, where I have lost sleep with previous providers.
Rep: Understood. We support local earned income tax withholding in Pennsylvania.
Linnea: Which codes? The rate depends on where the employee lives, not where they work, as I understand it. How does your system get the residence code correct when someone moves in the middle of the year?
Rep: We would need to confirm how the system handles the residence change. I would have to check with our tax team.
Priya Santangelo (IT Manager): From the systems side, can you show me where the address change comes into the payroll tax logic? Is it automatic from the employee record?
Rep: I believe so, but I do not want to say it with certainty.
Linnea: There is another case. We have a driver based in Ohio who lives in Kentucky. I would like to know whether the reciprocity form is handled in the system or on paper.
Rep: I would also need to confirm that one.
Linnea: I appreciate your honesty. I will say that your price was reasonable, a little more than Corvane's, which I do not mind. But I need these answers to be firm before I can recommend you.
Rep: I will get you written responses.
Linnea: Thank you. I will review them, but I am leaning elsewhere.

Rep: Priya, Beatrix, thanks for jumping on, I know the demo was only yesterday.
Priya Santangelo (HR Generalist): Yeah, that was fast, which I liked, although now I've had one night to think and I woke up with more questions. Okay, so, five states. Let me think out loud. Our newest hire is a remote dispatcher in Georgia. We've never had anyone in Georgia.
